title: Jeremiah 17:19–27
context: The LORD tells Jeremiah to stand in the gates of Jerusalem and address the kings of Judah and all the people about the Sabbath. They are not to carry burdens in or out on the Sabbath or do any work, but keep it holy as commanded. Their fathers did not listen. If they obey, kings on David's throne will enter the gates and the city will remain, with worshipers bringing offerings to the LORD's house. If not, the LORD will kindle an unquenchable fire in the gates. Nehemiah 13:15–22 later describes Nehemiah confronting Sabbath trade at the gates of Jerusalem.

verses.text: The LORD said this to me: “Go and stand in the gate of the children of the people, through which the kings of Judah come in and by which they go out, and in all the gates of Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes: "The LORD said this to me." Arminian readers see Jeremiah sent to the public gates, where kings and people pass, so that the message about the Sabbath reaches everyone.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the location matters: the gates were places of trade and public life. The LORD's word confronts the community where its daily choices are made.

verses.text: Tell them, ‘Hear the LORD’s word, you kings of Judah, all Judah, and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, that enter in by these gates:
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah is to say, "Hear the LORD’s word, you kings of Judah." Arminian readers see the call addressed to kings, all Judah, and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem. Everyone shares responsibility.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the kings are named first. Leaders bear special responsibility for the community's faithfulness. Both traditions see this address as including the whole people.

verses.text: The LORD says, “Be careful, and bear no burden on the Sabbath day, nor bring it in by the gates of Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, "Be careful, and bear no burden on the Sabbath day." Arminian readers see a concrete command: no carrying loads through Jerusalem's gates on the Sabbath.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the command applies the Sabbath law to the city's commerce. They connect it with Exodus 20:8, "Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy."

verses.text: Don’t carry a burden out of your houses on the Sabbath day. Don’t do any work, but make the Sabbath day holy, as I commanded your fathers.
verses.arminianNotes: "Don’t carry a burden out of your houses on the Sabbath day." Arminian readers see the command extended to homes as well as gates: "make the Sabbath day holy, as I commanded your fathers."
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the Sabbath command is presented as old, given to the fathers. Jeremiah is calling the people back to what they already knew, not giving a new law.

verses.text: But they didn’t listen. They didn’t turn their ear, but made their neck stiff, that they might not hear, and might not receive instruction.
verses.arminianNotes: "But they didn’t listen." Arminian readers see the fathers' stubborn refusal: they "made their neck stiff" so they would not hear or receive instruction.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the fathers' refusal echoes the stubborn heart of 16:12. The people's history of not listening frames the choice now set before them.

verses.text: It will happen, if you diligently listen to me,” says the LORD, “to bring in no burden through the gates of this city on the Sabbath day, but to make the Sabbath day holy, to do no work therein;
verses.arminianNotes: "It will happen, if you diligently listen to me," says the LORD. Arminian readers see a real condition: if the people keep the Sabbath holy, blessing will follow.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the promise is tied to diligent listening. Both traditions read the Sabbath blessing and warning here within Israel's covenant, without restating the site's existing notes on law and gospel.

verses.text: then there will enter in by the gates of this city kings and princes sitting on David’s throne, riding in chariots and on horses, they and their princes, the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem; and this city will remain forever.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD promises that "there will enter in by the gates of this city kings and princes sitting on David’s throne." Arminian readers see the blessing of obedience: a lasting kingdom and a city that "will remain forever."
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the promise connects Sabbath faithfulness with the Davidic throne and the city's future. They read it within Jeremiah's larger hope for David's line, without pressing details.

verses.text: They will come from the cities of Judah, and from the places around Jerusalem, from the land of Benjamin, from the lowland, from the hill country, and from the South, bringing burnt offerings, sacrifices, meal offerings, and frankincense, and bringing sacrifices of thanksgiving to the LORD’s house.
verses.arminianNotes: "They will come from the cities of Judah." Arminian readers see worshipers streaming from every region to bring offerings and "sacrifices of thanksgiving to the LORD’s house."
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that true Sabbath keeping leads to joyful worship. The picture is of a whole land gathered around the LORD's house in gratitude.

verses.text: But if you will not listen to me to make the Sabbath day holy, and not to bear a burden and enter in at the gates of Jerusalem on the Sabbath day, then I will kindle a fire in its gates, and it will devour the palaces of Jerusalem. It will not be quenched.” ’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: "But if you will not listen to me to make the Sabbath day holy." Arminian readers see the alternative: refusing to obey brings a fire that "will devour the palaces of Jerusalem."
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the fire "will not be quenched," echoing 17:4 and 4:4. The book later reports Jerusalem's burning (Jeremiah 39 and 52; 2 Kings 25), which these notes name without harmonizing.
